# Introduction to APIs and How Apps Talk to Each Other

## Overview
Behind every automation is an API (Application Programming Interface), which is simply the agreed-upon way one piece of software talks to another. Think of it like a restaurant menu: the API lists exactly what you can ask for and how to ask for it, and the app kitchen prepares the response. Automations work because the apps you connect (Gmail, Slack, a CRM) expose APIs that Zapier, Make, and n8n call on your behalf. When you eventually build custom steps, you will call APIs directly, so understanding the basics now pays off forever. Communication happens over HTTP using a small set of methods: GET fetches data (get me this customer), POST creates something (add a new record), PUT/PATCH updates, and DELETE removes. Each request can include headers (metadata like your authentication key), query parameters (filters in the URL like ?status=active), and a body (the data you are sending, usually JSON). The server replies with a response and a status code - 200 means success, 201 means created, 400 means you sent something wrong, 401 means you are not authenticated, 404 means not found, and 500 means the server errored. Being able to read an API's documentation - finding the endpoint URL, the required method, the parameters, and the authentication - is a core automation-engineer skill, because whenever a no-code tool does not have a ready-made action, you will drop down to a generic HTTP request and read the docs yourself.

## Deep Dive
This module covers: What an API is (a menu apps use to talk); HTTP methods: GET, POST, PUT, DELETE; Requests, responses, and status codes; Headers, query parameters, and request body; Reading API documentation. Mastering these ideas is essential because they appear repeatedly in production AI systems.

### What You Will Learn
- The core theory behind today's topic.
- How to apply it using Python, NumPy, Pandas, or the relevant framework.
- How to evaluate results and avoid common mistakes.
- Where to find authoritative references when you need deeper detail.

### Real-World Context
In industry, these skills are used daily: data scientists clean messy survey data, AI engineers deploy models to REST APIs, and automation engineers orchestrate pipelines. Today's practical task simulates one of these real-world scenarios.

## Hands-On Practice
**Practical Task:** Using a free tool like Postman or the browser, make a GET request to a public API (e.g., https://api.github.com/users/torvalds) and identify the status code, headers, and the JSON body in the response.
**Mini Project:** Pick a public API (GitHub, OpenWeather, or JSONPlaceholder), read its docs, and make at least one GET and one POST-style request, documenting the endpoint, method, parameters, and the response you received.
**Assignment:** Write a short cheat-sheet explaining the four main HTTP methods and five common status codes in plain language with an example of each.

Complete all three sections. Each completed section earns points toward your CalibiAI Score. If you are unsure about any part, use the AI assessment popup to submit your work and receive dynamic feedback from DeepSeek.

## Common Mistakes to Avoid
Many beginners rush into coding before fully understanding the data. Others skip validation steps and overestimate model performance. This module helps you build the discipline of checking assumptions first, then applying algorithms systematically.

## Career Impact
The skills covered today are frequently tested in technical interviews and required in entry-level AI engineering roles. Building a portfolio that demonstrates mastery of these concepts will significantly improve your job prospects.

## Key Takeaways
1. Theory guides practice — understand before coding.
2. Clean data and clear metrics are more valuable than complex models.
3. Document your steps for reproducibility.
4. Communication matters: explain results to non-technical stakeholders.

- Read any research papers linked for deeper theory.
- Prepare questions for tomorrow's module.

- Check the GitHub repositories for working code examples.
